title: Gifts for Coin Collectors: For Someone Who Knows a Lot
summary: Gifts for coin collectors who know more than you do: the 2027 Red Book, ANA membership, a coin show trip, safe storage, and how to pick a coin they'd want.
body_markdown:
A serious collector can tell you the date, mint mark and grade of the coin they want next. You probably can't, and that's the whole problem with buying them one. The gifts for coin collectors least likely to miss don't depend on knowing that coin: the new 2027 Red Book, a membership in the American Numismatic Association, a day at a coin show, or storage that keeps a collection safe. A coin can still be the right present. It just has to come off their want list.


We run Pure, a marketplace for coins and bullion, so the two coin ideas at the end point to listings there. The other six we don't sell.


## Find out what they collect before you buy a coin


Collections are built toward something. Someone working through Morgan dollars by date and mint mark wants one specific coin, and a lovely Peace dollar does nothing for that set. Someone who buys modern proofs from the US Mint may have no use for a worn 1880s coin at all.


So before buying a coin, try to learn a few things from whoever knows them best. A partner might, or a friend from their coin club, or the dealer they buy from.


-


The series, and the specific date and mint mark they're missing. Many collectors keep a written want list.


-


Whether their coins are **slabbed** , sealed in a grading company's plastic holder, or kept raw in flips and albums.


-


Which grading service they prefer. Serious collectors mostly use PCGS or NGC, and plenty keep a set in one company's holders only.[How PCGS and NGC differ](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/liberty-bell-coin-grading-pcgs-vs-ngc) is worth a skim if you've never heard either name.


Sometimes none of it can be found out without spoiling the surprise. That's what the first six are for, and they work for almost anyone in the hobby.


## Gifts that don't depend on knowing their collection


### 1. The 2027 Red Book


*A Guide Book of United States Coins* , which everyone calls the Red Book, first came out in 1946. The[80th edition, dated 2027, shipped in late June 2026](https://www.coinnews.net/2026/05/25/80th-red-book/) with more than 13,000 listings, and Whitman also put out a collector's edition with extra coverage of this year's Semiquincentennial coins.


A collector who buys every edition may already own it. Ask, or go for the collector's edition, which is sold separately.


### 2. An ANA membership


The American Numismatic Association puts on two big annual coin shows, and members get in free. Membership also brings *The Numismatist* every month and $15 off a first year with NGC.[The ANA's join page](https://info.money.org/join) lists digital membership at $35 a year and $55 for the printed magazine by mail, and says more than 27,000 collectors belong.


Plenty of serious collectors are already members. If yours is, the print upgrade is the version of this gift that still lands.


### 3. A trip to a coin show


At a show a collector can walk table after table of dealers and hold coins before buying any of them. The ANA's[2027 convention schedule](https://www.money.org/events/future-conventions/) has the National Money Show in Virginia Beach, March 4 to 6, and the World's Fair of Money at the Donald E. Stephens Convention Center in Rosemont, Illinois, August 10 to 14.


This pairs well with number two, since members get in free. Travel and a hotel night is a present on its own, and so is the company. Smaller regional shows run all year when a flight is too much.


### 4. A grading membership


Sending coins to be graded directly takes a paid membership. At NGC, the free tier lets you track a collection but not submit.[NGC's membership page](https://www.ngccoin.com/join/) puts direct submission at the Associate level, $39 a year, and the Premium level at $159 with a $150 grading credit included.


Find out which service they use before buying this. A credit at NGC does nothing for someone who sends everything to PCGS.


### 5. Storage that won't hurt the coins


Here a gift can go wrong without anyone noticing for years. Many soft plastic flips contain PVC, and[NGC warns](https://www.ngccoin.com/news/article/1364/) that the PVC can leave residue on a coin and, left long enough, etch the surface. Its advice is hard, PVC-free flips, and only for short-term storage at that.


Slabbed coins go in a storage box sized for graded holders, which keeps them upright with the labels readable. Raw coins want archival albums or PVC-free holders. Check which kind they have first.


### 6. A better loupe


Anyone who looks closely at grades almost certainly owns a loupe. The gift here is an upgrade from the one they use, so find out what that is (a glance in their desk drawer works) and buy a step up from it. A cheap lens from a gift shop will end up in that drawer too.


## Coins, if you know what they're missing


### 7. A certified Morgan dollar


The original Morgan series ran from 1878 to 1904 and again in 1921, struck at five different mints, and plenty of collectors spend years on it.[What sets a Morgan's value](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/morgan-silver-dollar-value) covers the dates and mint marks if you want to follow along. A certified example is sealed in a holder by PCGS or NGC, its condition graded on the[1 to 70 Sheldon scale](https://www.ngccoin.com/coin-grading/grading-scale/) and the grade printed on the label.


A random date is a duplicate waiting to happen. Get the exact coin from their list, match the grading service they use, and buy that one.[Numismatic coins on Pure](https://www.collectpure.com/marketplace/featured/numismatic-coins) collects the certified and collectible coins currently listed, Morgans and proof Eagles included.


### 8. A proof Silver Eagle with its box and certificate


A collector of modern US Mint issues is the person for a proof American Silver Eagle. Collectors split on how much the original box and certificate of authenticity matter. If yours keeps Mint boxes on a shelf, get one listed with both. Recent issues include the[2025 privy-mark proofs](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/team-usa-privy-silver-eagle) marking the 250th anniversaries of the Army, the Navy and the Marine Corps, so check which ones they already have. For a collector who follows every Mint release, our[list of this year's US Mint gifts](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/gifts-for-us-mint-coin-collectors) covers the 2026 proof sets and the Liberty Bell pieces.


On Pure, every listing is a seller's ask, and every item is verified in house before it ships. Items that pass ship Pure Qualified, and shipping is insured. Leave enough time before the holiday that delivery isn't what you're waiting on.


## Questions people ask


### What does every coin collector need?


A reference for their series, a loupe, and storage that won't damage what they own. Past that, it depends entirely on what they collect, which is why the questions near the top of this post matter more than any list.


### What are coin collectors looking for right now?


The one you're shopping for is looking for whatever is next on their list, and no article can tell you what that is. Modern US collectors have had a busy 2026, though. The Mint is issuing[Semiquincentennial designs](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/semiquincentennial-coins-complete-guide) for the circulating quarter, dime and half dollar, alongside proof sets and commemorative Eagles. Ask whether they've finished.


### Is a coin a good gift for a coin collector?


When it's off their want list, yes, and it's probably the gift they'll remember. A coin picked without that list is the riskiest thing on this page. Serious collectors have opinions about eye appeal and holders that a gift-giver can't guess at.


### What's a good Christmas gift for a coin collector who has everything?


A membership, a show, or a book holds up well here, since none of them duplicates a coin. Both 2027 ANA shows fall after the holidays, so a printed note with the show dates and a hotel booking can go under the tree.


## Where to start


Knowing nothing about their collection, give the 2027 Red Book or an ANA membership. With the list in hand, buy one coin off it. If the list is all new Mint issues, start with the[US Mint gifts](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/gifts-for-us-mint-coin-collectors) post instead. For someone who stacks silver by the ounce rather than collecting coins, see[gifts for silver collectors](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/gifts-for-silver-collectors) .


The broader metal-gift list is[gold and silver gift ideas](https://www.collectpure.com/blog/gold-and-silver-gift-ideas) , with the pieces under $250 collected on[gold and silver gifts](https://www.collectpure.com/marketplace/featured/gold-silver-gifts) .
